rv.q: If you're feeling the autumn blues, seize your straw boater immediately and head to Kingston for this gorgeous burst of theatrical sunshine.
This is a vivid, panto-adjacent romp that delivers a huge dose of feelgood fun and a couple of moments of genuine pathos.
Slapstick dominates in an engaging evening that smooths the jagged oddness of the book.
Despite two-and-a-half hours of digressions, the story still remains buoyant.
Despite two-and-a-half hours of digressions, the story remains steadfastly buoyant.
I found this hectic vaudevillian take on Three Men in a Boat farcical for all the wrong reasons.
Three Men in a Boat is delightfully old-fashioned and anarchic British comedy at its very best: something we all need more of right now.
Funny, energetic and winningly performed, this busy adaptation loses its way whenever it reaches for insights beyond Jerome K. Jerome’s timeless original.
It's as if Christmas has come early to the Rose and while not a pantomime, this is a show with many of panto's credentials.

Writer Al Smith has taken Jerome K. Jerome’s famously episodic 1889 novel and shaped it into a fast-moving theatrical romp. Under Christopher Haydon’s direction Jonny Weldon, Bronté Barbé and Richard David-Caine throw themselves into the escalating chaos, more than ably supported by puppeteer Calum Donald-Bruce.

The novelty of the text is in its familiarity with smaller stops along the way; having thus inspired countless boat trips following the same pathway. Despite being written over a century ago, the characters and even the jokes still feel witty and relatable, delighting audiences in the absurdity of it all.

Having the journey begin in Kingston also gives the play a particularly fitting local connection. The play is an absolute visual treat, with a delightful production design that constantly finds new ways to make the stage part of the comedy.

For the most part, we are sucked into the whirlwind with joy. However, at times the tornado of turmoil is a little too tiresome, and a few scenes could be trimmed to prevent the performance from becoming stagnant.
It's messy, unpredictable and completely ridiculous — but somehow, that's exactly what makes it work.

cn.t: Critics find this madcap Thames adventure stupendously silly and entertaining, praising its energetic performances and witty musical additions. Most celebrate the chaotic fun, though some feel the gimmick-laden production overcomplicates Jerome's gentle comedy.
